name: LT1461AIS8-2.5#PBF
title: LT1461: micropower, low-dropout precision series voltage reference, 2.5 V to 5 V
summary: A bandgap series reference in SO-8 with fixed outputs of 2.5 V, 3 V, 3.3 V, 4.096 V or 5 V. Four grades span 0.04 % to 0.15 % initial accuracy and 3 to 20 ppm/°C drift; the part takes 35 µA typical, sources at least 50 mA, drops out at under 300 mV at 1 mA, and has a shutdown pin and thermal shutdown. LT1461AIS8-2.5#PBF is the A grade, 2.5 V, -40 °C to 85 °C part.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Supply input, from VOUT + 0.3 V up to 20 V; needs a bypass capacitor.

pins.name: SHDN
pins.function: Shutdown, active low. Left open or held at 2.4 V or more, the reference runs; at 0.8 V or less the output turns off. An internal 100 kΩ sits in series with this pin.

pins.name: VOUT
pins.function: Reference output; needs an output capacitor for stability.

notes: Note 4: the part is sensitive to electrostatic discharge. It has internal ESD protection, yet a large discharge can still harm or degrade it; handle it with ESD precautions.

Note 5: the coefficient is the spread between the highest and lowest output read at TMIN, room temperature and TMAX, divided by the temperature span: TC = (VOMAX – VOMIN)/(TMAX – TMIN). The slope at 25 °C is measured too.
Note 6: load regulation is taken with pulses, stepping from zero load to the stated current. Any output shift from a change in die temperature is a separate error to add.

Note 7: 0.1 Hz to 10 Hz peak-to-peak noise uses a one-pole 0.1 Hz high-pass and a two-pole 10 Hz low-pass, with the part in still air to keep thermocouple effects off its leads, over a 10 s test. The 10 Hz to 1 kHz figure uses a one-pole 10 Hz high-pass and a two-pole 1 kHz low-pass; the result is full-wave rectified and integrated over a set time, giving an average, which is scaled by 1.1 to RMS and by 0.88 for the filters' non-ideal passband.

Note 8: drift falls off roughly logarithmically with time, so change after the first 1000 h is much smaller; the second 1000 h typically drifts under a third as much as the first, and less again after that. Stress between the IC and the board from assembly also affects it.

Note 9: hysteresis comes from package stress and depends on whether the part was last hotter or colder. The output is always read at 25 °C, with the part taken hot or cold between readings. It scales roughly with the square of the temperature swing, and is usually no concern for normal operating swings where the instrument might be stored hot or cold.

circuits.title: Basic connection
circuits.description: The minimum circuit: a 1 µF capacitor across the supply input and a 2 µF capacitor across the output, with SHDN left open so the reference stays on. The input may sit anywhere from VOUT + 0.3 V to 20 V.

circuits.title: Low power 16-bit A/D
circuits.description: An LT1461-2.5 sets the reference for an LTC2400 converter. Both chips run from one VCC rail; the reference draws about 35 µA and the converter about 200 µA. The reference output carries 1 µF to ground and feeds VREF; the analog input has 0.1 µF to ground; FO is grounded and SCK, SDO and CS form the SPI port.
notes: Converter noise with this reference: 1.1 ppmRMS (16 µVP-P) at 0 V input, 1.6 ppmRMS (24 µVP-P) at VREF/2 and 2.5 ppmRMS (36 µVP-P) at full scale.

where.VOMAX: highest output among the readings at TMIN, room and TMAX

equations.name: Arrhenius acceleration factor
equations.note: With 30 °C use (303 K) and 130 °C test (403 K), AF = 767. Long-term drift measured at 30 °C (60 ppm per 1000 h) and at 130 °C (120 ppm per 1000 h) does not follow this factor: 120 ppm/767 would predict 0.156 ppm per 1000 h, about 0.39 µV on a 2.5 V part.

equations.name: Load regulation error
equations.note: A 50 mA step on the 2.5 V part moves the output about 1.5 mV.

equations.name: Junction temperature
equations.note: LT1461-2.5 with 17.5 V across it at 50 mA dissipates 875 mW, a 166 °C rise, giving 191 °C from 25 °C; thermal shutdown holds the junction near 150 °C instead.

operation.text: A low-dropout bandgap series reference with curvature correction and trimmed thin-film resistors. It runs on 35 µA typical yet can source 50 mA, so it serves both battery-powered references and precision regulators. Five output voltages; all parts work from -40 °C to 125 °C.

A grade: 0.04 % and 3 ppm/°C. B: 0.06 % and 7 ppm/°C. C: 0.08 % and 12 ppm/°C, each in a 0 °C to 70 °C (C suffix) or -40 °C to 85 °C (I suffix) version. D grade (H suffix, -40 °C to 125 °C): 0.15 % and 20 ppm/°C, with looser line and load regulation limits; its load regulation is specified to 10 mA, and the 50 mA dropout figure applies to I and C temperature grades only.

Both pins need a capacitor for the part to be stable. On the input, bypass capacitors of nearby parts suffice if they lie within 2 inches. The output capacitor is the loop's frequency compensation and must be present: 1 µF non-polar for loads up to 1 mA, 2 µF or more for heavier loads up to 75 mA.

It delivers 50 mA with VIN = VOUT + 2.5 V, and more with a higher input. Thermal regulation (output shift from die temperature gradients set by load or input change) is too small to measure; at 200 mW of sudden dissipation the output shows no thermal error. Thermal shutdown turns the part off above a 150 °C junction.
Pulling pin 3 low cuts off the load current. Open or at 2.4 V and up, the part runs normally. Shut down, it draws at most 35 µA. Coming out of shutdown the output settles in about 200 µs.

Bending and heat stress in a board can move the output of a surface-mount reference, more so than other packages, and soldering itself shifts it. Placing the part near a short edge or a corner of the board, and orienting it with its leads along the board's long side, reduces this, as the leads take up the strain. In a flexing test two parts mounted with leads along the long dimension moved 125 µV (50 ppm), and two mounted across it 250 µV (100 ppm). Slots cut around three sides of the part, with the leads leaving on the fourth and the tongue pointing along the board, brought the shift from about 100 ppm to nearly zero.

Drift was measured on three parts soldered to boards in a 30 °C oven, read with an 8.5-digit DVM through a scanner, with a Fluke 732A standard as a cross-check. Typical drift is 60 ppm in the first 1000 h at 30 °C and 120 ppm at 130 °C; the trend flattens toward 2000 h. Accelerated high-temperature tests do not predict it. Assembly stress between IC and board also affects drift.

The hysteresis distributions are worst-case results from 35 socketed parts after repeated cycling; wider swings give more. The -40 °C to 25 °C result depends on where the part came from, since a trip to 125 °C leaves stress not fully relieved at the 25 °C reading. Parts IR-soldered to a board and cycled -40 °C to 85 °C show the effect of board stress.
Forty parts reflowed onto a board moved by -110 ppm on average; twelve days later they had typically recovered 45 ppm toward their starting value as solder stress relaxed.

At high dissipation thermal shutdown limits the junction to about 150 °C, but the excursion leaves a hysteresis shift, typically -135 ppm and possibly more, which can take the 25 °C output outside its accuracy limit. For the best accuracy keep the junction at or below 125 °C.
